draft.title: Peace in Christianity
card: Christians follow the teaching of Jesus. In the Sermon on the Mount, he says "Blessed are the peacemakers", so Christians are called to work actively for peace.
Jesus also taught his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who treat them badly. This means answering hostility with care, not revenge.
Christians often link peace with justice. Many see real peace as more than the absence of fighting, because it also needs fair treatment for people.
Many churches act on this belief. They may run aid programs, speak out against war and unfair laws, or support refugees and people in need.
draft.remember: Christians are called to love enemies and be peacemakers, and many churches act for peace and justice.

a.q: Which teaching of Jesus do Christians draw on when they try to answer hostility with care?
opts: Love your enemies
Blessed are the rich
Seek peace through craving
Submit to the will of Allah
a.why: Jesus taught his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who treat them badly. The other options come from other ideas, not from this teaching of Jesus, and none of them is about answering hostility with care.
a.clue: Think of what Jesus said about how to treat enemies.

b.q: A church in Newcastle runs a refugee support program and speaks out against an unfair law. Which Christian belief best explains this?
opts: Peace needs justice as well as an end to fighting
Peace means only staying out of all public debates
Peace comes only from private prayer and silence
Peace is the job of governments, not of churches
b.why: Many Christians link peace with justice, so they act to help people and challenge unfair treatment. Private prayer matters to Christians, but the card says many churches also act in public, so the prayer-only option is wrong.
b.clue: Look for the belief that joins peace to fair treatment.

b.best: Peace needs justice as well as an end to fighting

problems.detail: The clue ('what Jesus said about how to treat enemies') points straight to 'Love your enemies'. The distractors are also obviously wrong: one is an inverted Buddhist idea, one names Allah, and 'Blessed are the rich' is not a teaching of Jesus. A student can answer without knowing the idea.
Too easy for Year 12 HSC. No distractor is a plausible Christian teaching, so the question tests very little.
The right option stands out because it is the only one with no absolute word. Three distractors say 'only' or 'not', so they are easy to rule out without knowing the idea.
The clue ('joins peace to fair treatment') nearly restates the right option, which gives the answer away.

a.q: In Jesus's teaching, what does it mean to love your enemies?
opts: Answering hostility with care rather than revenge
Returning harm equal to the harm you received
Keeping well away from people who cause harm
Forgiving enemies once they have apologised
a.why: Jesus taught his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who treat them badly, which means responding to hostility with care, not revenge. Forgiving after an apology is tempting, but the teaching does not wait for the enemy to change first.
a.clue: Does the teaching wait for the other person to change?

b.q: A church in Newcastle runs a refugee support program and speaks out against an unfair law. Which Christian belief best explains this?
opts: Real peace includes justice, not just an end to fighting
Real peace is reached once fighting between groups ends
Real peace comes mainly from private prayer and calm
Real peace means keeping order and obeying the law
b.why: Many Christians see real peace as more than the absence of fighting, because it also needs fair treatment for people. That is why churches support refugees and challenge unfair laws. The view that peace arrives once fighting ends is tempting, but no fighting is involved here, so it cannot explain the church's actions.
b.clue: No one is fighting here, so why would the church act?

a.best: Answering hostility with care rather than revenge

b.best: Real peace includes justice, not just an end to fighting
